fact: Adult cats sleep around 12 to 16 hours a day.
Cats purr when content, but also sometimes when stressed or in pain.
Adult cats rarely meow at each other; meowing is mostly a way to talk to people.
A cat's whiskers are roughly as wide as its body and help it judge narrow gaps.
Cats have a 'righting reflex' that lets them twist in mid-air to land on their feet.
A cat can jump up to about five times its own height.
Cats cannot taste sweetness; they lack a working sweet taste receptor.
Most adult cats are lactose intolerant, so a saucer of milk can upset their stomach.
Every cat's nose has a unique pattern of ridges, a bit like a fingerprint.
Cats were revered in ancient Egypt, and the goddess Bastet was often shown with a cat's head.
Cats were first domesticated in the Near East, roughly 10,000 years ago, around early farming villages.
A slow blink from a cat is a sign of trust; people can slow-blink back.
Kneading with the front paws is a habit left over from kittenhood nursing.
Cats like boxes because small enclosed spaces help them feel safe and warm.
Cats spend up to half of their waking hours grooming themselves.
A cat's tongue is covered in tiny backward-facing hooks called papillae.
Cats can hear higher-pitched sounds than dogs or humans.
Cats see well in dim light thanks to a reflective layer behind the retina, the tapetum lucidum.
Each cat ear has over 30 muscles and can rotate about 180 degrees.
Most cats have five toes on each front paw and four on each back paw.
A cat holding its tail straight up is usually greeting you in a friendly way.
Kittens are born with their eyes closed; they open after about one to two weeks.
Kittens are born with blue eyes; their adult eye colour develops over the first months.
Even well-fed cats keep their hunting instinct, which is why they stalk toys.
Many cats prefer running water, which is why some drink from taps.
A domestic cat can sprint at around 48 km/h over short distances.
Catnip affects roughly half to two-thirds of cats; the response is inherited.
Cats were kept on ships for centuries to keep rats and mice away from the food stores.
Cats have a free-floating collarbone, which helps them squeeze through gaps their head fits through.
Cats sometimes bring prey home to their people, possibly treating them like inexperienced hunters.
